assumptions: The founder can avoid conflicts with the current employer and use no confidential employer data or relationships.
The initial offer is narrowed to one commodity and sold as a paid evidence-gap audit before substantial software investment.
Qualified compliance specialists can be contracted within the stated capital envelope, while the founder continues working approximately 20 hours weekly.
No durable cross-customer data moat is credited unless importer and supplier agreements expressly permit lawful reuse of derived evidence.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Signed paid pilots with importers in one commodity; measured audit-to-subscription conversion, sales cycle and channel CAC; referral agreements with brokers or ERP consultants; shipment-level delivery hours, geospatial and expert-review costs, gross margin and error rates; renewal evidence; and contracts granting durable access plus lawful reuse of derived supplier data would support a higher score.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: EUDR creates a concrete coordination problem around supplier documents, plot geolocation, validation, versioning and official-system handoff. Buyer examples support the need, but the mechanism is already recognized and served by multiple vendors rather than being a uniquely overlooked insight.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Operators face a mandatory pre-market due-diligence event, depend on upstream suppliers, and there is evidence that firms adopt software or commission ERP workflows. However, no importer has paid or committed to this candidate, free tooling covers some readiness work, and the operator retains substantive responsibility.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Upfront implementation plus recurring subscriptions could provide favorable cash conversion and repeat revenue as shipments, suppliers and rules change. The proposed price, 60-75% contribution margin, CAC, retention and payback are unvalidated, while specialist review, supplier support, security, insurance and regulatory maintenance may materially raise delivery costs; public substitutes also indicate price pressure.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: A single commodity and CEE importer segment is a sensible, testable beachhead with a deadline-driven need and potential local-language service differentiation. Its economically reachable size after simplification is unknown, and the initial definition spanning several commodities is too broad for specialized evidence and supplier workflows.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Polish-language exception handling and a managed-service layer could win a niche, but incumbents already offer supplier portals, validation, audit trails, ERP connectors and official-system workflows. The candidate presently controls neither customer relationships nor exclusive data, making a dominant position difficult to establish.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful commodity wedge could extend across other covered commodities, CEE geographies, ERP integrations, supplier readiness, risk monitoring and adjacent trade-compliance workflows. Expansion would require new commodity expertise and supplier onboarding, and confidentiality or reuse restrictions may prevent the evidence graph from transferring cleanly.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: A supplier-resolution graph and evidence-quality benchmarks could compound only if contracts permit durable cross-customer reuse. No data license, exclusivity, renewal protection or transferable right exists today; suppliers and importers own the inputs, the Commission controls submission infrastructure, and the workflow is replaceable or bundleable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A managed gateway may be more convenient than self-service software for importers needing supplier chasing, geolocation QA and Polish-language exception support. No measured improvement in accuracy, speed, total cost or risk reduction establishes a compelling advantage, while lower-priced competitors and free tooling cover substantial portions of the job.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The December 2026 and June 2027 application dates create immediate urgency, and the July 2026 scope and system changes reinforce demand for maintained workflows rather than static checklists. Simplification and further rule changes can also shrink or reshape the opportunity.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Customs brokers and ERP consultants are plausible concentrated referral channels, supplemented by targeted outbound. There is no referral agreement, qualified pipeline, conversion evidence or validated CAC, and prospective partners may demand revenue share, build competing modules or favor established platforms.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data-science background, AI leverage, available capital and part-time capacity fit a narrow audit-first launch. Execution still requires regulatory judgment, geospatial validation, security, professional-liability controls, importer authorization and persistent supplier cooperation; high-touch exceptions could conflict with part-time operation and assumed margins.

highest_value_structural_change: Make a commodity-specific broker or ERP partner the repeatable acquisition wedge and contract for permissioned supplier-data reuse, turning paid audits into a shared evidence network with demonstrably lower onboarding cost for each additional importer.
main_structural_strength: A legally mandated, recurring evidence workflow with near-term deadlines creates a real purchase trigger that fits an audit-first, capital-light entry strategy.
primary_score_limiter: The business does not control the critical data, customer channel or official submission infrastructure, while established and inexpensive substitutes already cover much of the proposed workflow.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Existing vendors already combine supplier participation, validation, audit trails, ERP connectivity and official-system workflows, with public prices as low as €62.50-€187.50 per month or €149 per workspace, while a free open-source toolkit covers portions of due-diligence design.
